Tttm'S A SOHO 

by Helen Tuttle 

Where there’s a camp there’s a song. 
You will hear it around the campfire, 
at the meal-table, and along the hikers’ 
road. Singing has its proper places 
through the day—whether in displays 
of sheer enthusiasm or in moments of 
solemn worship. Girls and boys who 
sing nowhere else will learn to sing at 
camp. They love it. Give them a tune, 
and you’ll hear them humming it as 
they do the dishes. 

Singing at camp is no mere time- 
filler. It helps to carry the message of 
camp itself. Watch the quiet youngster 
lose his shyness in an action song. 
Observe the boisterous one stilled by 
the loveliness of vesper singing. 

Sometimes camp singing is just plain 
fun. It may even border on shouting 
whether youngsters get carried away by 
a sprightly tune or marching tempo. 
Each tries to be heard above the others 
in a competitive atmosphere which 
sounds like bedlam. Don’t be alarmed; 
there’s a place for that experience. But 
we should aim to lead boys and girls 
into far richer experiences of song. 
Help them appreciate singing as a 
means of expressing every shade of feel¬ 
ing. Give them the satisfaction which 
comes from co-operative singing in 
rounds and even harmony. 

The best camp singing doesn’t often 
just happen. It is a product of plan¬ 
ning and inspiration by a leader who 
loves the job and a group of campers 
who will soon catch on. 

Plan Group Singing 

“Community Singing” is an over-all 
term which refers to the many situa¬ 
tions where people sing together. It 
ranges all the way from the folk-song 
sung by people in their natural setting 
of home and occupation to the helter- 
skelter sing-song of a get-acquainted 
session. The most characteristic singing 


at camp I prefer to call “group¬ 
singing”. This type of situation gives 
the leader a chance to work out a full 
programme of singing. The leader gets 
to know the capacities of each member 
and is able to draw these out more 
fully. This is possible when a group 
is living and working together for a 
period of days. Here are a few things 
to remember when planning group 
singing: 

1. Always have a good choice of 
songs; always variety and more 
than you can use. 

2. Make a new list for each session, 
bearing in mind the wisdom of 
learning new songs and repeating 
familiar ones. 

3. Classify your songs for easy refer¬ 
ence. Examples: folk songs, rousing 
songs, rounds, action songs, quiet 
songs, spirituals, hymns, etc. 

4. Plan a good order of songs to suit 
the period involved. One order 
is more suitable at meal-time; 
another for the camp-fire. 

5. It is often helpful to have a Com¬ 
mittee of campers to work with 
the leader. Discuss with them the 
place of singing at camp and ask 
for their suggestions. 

Song Leadership 

Let me suggest a few qualities a song 
leader should cultivate and some simple 
rules to follow: 

1. Know your songs thoroughly, 
words and tunes. 

2. Know your appearance when in 
action. Be clear in your explana¬ 
tion and smooth in direction. A 
jumpy, fast-beating time will only 
detract from the song. Be as incon¬ 
spicuous as possible in manner. 

3. Watch your own attitude. A good 
leader is patient, pleasant, and 
will see the humour in mistakes, 
whether of the group or himself. 
Always be positive. Make favour¬ 
able comments first, and sugges¬ 
tions for improvement second. 

4. Do not confuse campers by singing 
harmony parts yourself, unless you

arc obviously aiding one section of 
the group. 

5. Be open to the requests of camp¬ 
ers for the old favourites—but also 
very ready with your own sugges¬ 
tions to teach a new song. Accept 
theirs and they’ll take yours. 

6. It’s better to suggest than to 
demand. 

7. Be on your toes and the pro¬ 
gramme won’t drag. 

Teaching a New Song 

To teach a new song: 

1. Use a blackboard, if possible, so 
that all eyes are then on the leader 
and words at once. 

2. Begin by listening to the piano 
once, then the leader and piano 
once, then lah-lahing together. 

3. Let the leader and those who think 
they know the song sing it through 
once, while the others are encour¬ 
aged merely to imagine themselves 
singing. 

4. Everybody sing once; then drop 
until the next session.

from page 132 

f Hot Potato: use a bean bag which 
must be tossed round or across a 
circle very quickly. Tt’ stands in the 
centre and attempts to touch the bag. 
Whoever lets him becomes ‘it’. 

J Snatch. Two lines number in oppo¬ 
site directions, and separated by 
about six feet. A dumb-bell is placed 
in the centre. The referee calls out 
a number and both the persons must 
try to retrieve the dumb-bell. The 
one who hasn’t got it is allowed to 
tag the other. Tagging doesn’t count 
if the dumb-bell has been dropped. 
The team which retrieves the dumb¬ 
bell without being tagged gets one 
point; or the team which tags gets 
one point. 

Sardines: first person hides; first 
person to find him must hide in the 
same place with him; ad continuum.
